Meah Abdul Gafur with Farid Ahmed, Advocates ------- For the Petitioner. 
S R Karmaker with M L Gomaz, Advocates ------- For the Opposite Party.
parties:
Rahima Begum ------- Petitioner.
Vs.
Md. Abdul Baten.  ------- Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
2. The property in dispute consists of a homestead land 11 acres in area upon which stood a tin-shed and a kitchen, bearing Plot No. 273 appertaining to khatian No. 326 of mouza Kaoraid under PS Sreepur which the applicant Abdul Baten purchased on 13.6.70 for a consideration of Tk. 2000.00. Abdul Baten sold the homestead to the petitioner Rahima Begum by a registered Kabala dated 5.4.74 for a consideration of Taka 10, 000'00. On 10.7.76 he filed an application under section 4 of the said Ordinance before the authorised Officer, that is local Circle Officer (Rev), praying for restoration of the homestead on the allegation of the transfer having been made during the period of economic distress for reasons of such distress. Rahima Begum appeared and filed a written objection denying Abdul Baten's allegations. Two witnesses namely Nirod Chand Saha identifier of the Kabala dated 5.4.74 and one Abdur Rahim Fakir were examined on behalf of Abdul Baten and six witnesses including the scribe of the kabala were examined on behalf of the other side. Neither the parties nor Rahima Begum's husband examined themselves. It however appears that the authorised officer did not record the deposition of the witnesses but merely noted in the order sheets the substance of the statements made by the witnesses on behalf of the respective parties. He rejected the application holding that the transfer could not come within the mischief of the said Ordinance by reason of the fact that it was not made for reasons of economic distress but for purchase of land elsewhere. 

 3. Against this order Abdul Baten preferred an appeal (No. 4 of 1977) under section 8 of the said Ordinance before the Munsif, 6th Court, Dhaka, which on transfer to Upazila Sreepur was renumbered as Misc. Appeal No. 73 of 1983. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record has held that being a homestead as defined in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act the property is agricultural land within the contemplation of the said Ordinance and that the transfer in question was made during the period of economic distress for reasons of such distress. He has accordingly allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the authorised officer with the observation that the appellant Abdul Baten is entitled to have his alienaled land in question restored as per provisions of the said Ordinance. There is, however, no direction in the order as to the re-payment of the amount of the consideration money as provided in section 4(2)(b) thereof. It is against this appellate judgment and order that Rahima Begum has moved this Court and obtained the instant Rule. 

 5. The second point raised on behalf of the petitioner is that the transfer was not made for reasons of economic distress within the contemplation of law. He submits that it is clear from the very recital of the document that the transfer was made with a view to collect fund to purchase some hinds elsewhere. He further submits that after the transfer the applicant was left with more-than 3 acres of agricultural lands. In reply Mr. Karmaker, on the other hand, has referred to the applicant's counter-affidavit wherein it is stated that the recital in the document was made at the dictation of the other side and as a matter of fact he had no intention to purchase nor had he actually purchased any land with the money. He submits that it could not be denied in the affidavit-in-reply that the applicant did not purchase any land. He has also submitted that there is nothing on record to show that after the transfer the applicant was left with more than 3 acres of agricultural lands. In this connection he has referred to section 3(2) of the said Ordinance and also to the assertion of the applicant to the effect that he was left with only 1.01-1/2 acres of lands. 

 7. It is next contended by the learned advocate for the petitioner that the court below has failed to consider that the disputed property is not an agricultural land within the contemplation of the said Ordinance. According to him, although the agricultural land includes homestead yet it not being a homestead of an agriculturist nor being held for agricultural purposes the homestead is not the one within the purview of the law. He submits that the vendor is a ration dealer and as such a businessman and not an agriculturist. Mr. Karmaker submits that according to the said Ordinance, a homestead as defined in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act falls within the definition of agricultural land and that the homestead in the said Act has been defined to mean a dwelling house with the land under it and there is no qualification attached to it, although in the inclusive clause of the definition some qualification regarding use for the purpose of agriculture or horticulture has been attached to out-building. 

 "homestead means a dwelling house with the land under it together with any courtyard, garden, tank, place of worship and private burial or cremation ground attached and appertaining to such dwelling house, and includes any out building used for the purpose of enjoying the dwelling house or for purpose connected with agriculture or horticulture and such lands within well-defined limits, whether vacant or not, as are treated to be appurtenant thereto. "It is clear from this definition that if it is a dwelling house then the question whether the dwelling house belongs to agriculturist or non-agriculturist is not at all relevant. Even otherwise a ration dealer is not necessarily a non-agriculturist. There is therefore no escape from the conclusion that the disputed property is a homestead as defined in the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and as such an agricultural land within contemplation of the said Ordinance. The learned Munsif has also proceeded with the assumption that it is an agricultural land although without any elaborate discussion, possibly because this point was not seriously agitated before him". 

 11. In the instant case, however, there has been no decision by the lower forums as to the net income or the date of receipt of consideration money. It is not the case of the applicant that the transferee has derived any income from the disputed property. So no necessity arises for determination by the authorized officer of the net income. But the transferee appears to have claimed that the consideration money was paid on different dates in the year 1973, although the applicant denies this. From the order date 23.7.77 in the order sheets of the authorized officer it appears that the witnesses examined on behalf of the transferee stated that the consideration money was paid before the registration but it does not appear that it was so paid in installments on different dates in the year 1973 as contended by the transferee. Neither the transferee nor her husband who in normal circumstances must have made the actual payment has not examined himself or herself before the authorized officer. Thus there is no evidence in support of the transferee's case of the payment having been made in 1973. So also there having been no satisfactory evidence the applicant's plea that the consideration was paid some time after the registration of the kabala cannot be believed. There is therefore no scope to take a view other than what would follow from the normal conduct of the parties, and the payment in such circumstances must be held to have been made at the time of execution and registration of the document that is on 5.4.75. Thus there is no difficulty on the question of determination of net income or the date of receipt of the consideration. The required particulars being thus available it may be safely held that the technical omission of compliance with the requirement of law in the impugned order does not warrant remand of the case and that the omission could be supplied by the revisional court in case of course the impugned order is maintained. 

 "6. No eviction, etc, from the homestead -Any land used as a homestead by its owner in the rural area shall be exempted from all legal processes, including seizure, distress, attachment or sale by any office, court or any other authority and the owner of such land shall not be divested or dispossessed of the land or evicted there form by any means: Provided that nothing in this section shall apply to the acquisition of such homestead under any law."
